questions.question: Which primitives belong in a from-scratch `numth` number-theory library?
options: gcd, mod_inverse, mod_pow, prime test, factor, CRT, sqrt mod p, totient
AES key schedule, SHA-256 compression, ChaCha20 cipher, BLAKE3 hashing
Elliptic curve point addition, scalar multiplication, curve point validation
Lattice basis reduction (LLL), shortest vector, closest vector heuristics
questions.explanation: Number-theory library exposes the primitives from Phase 1: arithmetic mod n, gcd/inverse, primality, factoring, CRT, sqrt mod p, totient/Carmichael.

questions.question: Why expose `mod_inverse(a, n)` as a separate API rather than computing via Fermat each time?
options: Fermat-method works only when n is prime; gcd-method handles composite n too
Fermat-method is slower than EEA-based inverse for all input sizes uniformly
Fermat-method requires φ(n) which is private; exposing it would leak the key
Fermat-method returns negative residues; users must normalize the result manually
questions.explanation: Fermat a^(p−2) mod p only works for prime p. EEA-based mod_inverse handles general n given gcd(a, n) = 1 (or raises).

questions.question: Which library API is the right tool for RSA decryption: `pow(c, d, n)` vs `mod_pow(c, d, n)` (custom)?
options: Use `pow(c, d, n)` — Python's built-in implementation is faster and well-tested
Use `mod_pow(c, d, n)` — custom code is more secure because it avoids GMP backdoors
Use either — performance and correctness are identical for cryptographic input sizes
Use neither — RSA decryption should never call modular exponentiation directly
questions.explanation: `pow(c, d, n)` is a heavily tested built-in modular-exponentiation path. Always prefer it for correctness and speed. Hand-rolled `mod_pow` is for teaching; never ship it.

questions.question: Your `numth.factor(n)` should fall back through which algorithms in order?
options: Trial division (small primes) → Pollard rho → Pollard p−1 → Quadratic Sieve → GNFS
AKS (primality) → Miller-Rabin (primality) → BSGS (DLP) → Pollard rho (factor)
Quadratic Sieve → Pollard rho → Trial division — start expensive then bail out cheap
Random sampling of divisors — uniform over [2, √n] until gcd > 1 emerges from chance
questions.explanation: Cost-ordered: trial divide by primes up to ~10⁶, then Pollard rho/p−1 (good for n with smooth or moderate factors), then QS for ~50–100 digit n, GNFS beyond. Detect prime at any step via Miller-Rabin.

questions.question: Why must `numth.is_prime(n)` use Miller-Rabin instead of Fermat?
options: Carmichael numbers fool Fermat for every coprime base; Miller-Rabin bounds liars ≤ 1/4
Fermat requires gcd(a, n) = 1 always; Miller-Rabin skips that prerequisite step
Miller-Rabin is faster than Fermat for all input sizes due to its strong test
Fermat returns probabilistic results while Miller-Rabin is fully deterministic
questions.explanation: Fermat liars are unbounded for Carmichael composites. Miller-Rabin proven ≤ 1/4 liars. For n < ~3·10²⁴, twelve fixed bases give deterministic MR.

questions.question: Your library exposes `mod_sqrt(a, p)`. Which fallback chain should it use?
options: If p ≡ 3 (mod 4): a^((p+1)/4) mod p; else: Tonelli-Shanks loop on general odd p
Always Tonelli-Shanks regardless of p mod 4 to keep one code path simple
Always closed form a^((p+1)/4) and document failure when p ≡ 1 (mod 4)
Trial: enumerate every x in [1, p − 1] and test x² ≡ a until match found
questions.explanation: p ≡ 3 (mod 4) → closed form, no loop. p ≡ 1 (mod 4) → Tonelli-Shanks. Reject when (a/p) = −1. Standard structure in well-implemented libraries.

questions.question: What should `numth.crt(residues, moduli)` validate before computing?
options: All moduli pairwise coprime; raise if any pair shares a non-trivial common factor
All residues fit in 64-bit integers; raise on overflow to avoid silent corruption
All moduli are prime; CRT does not apply to composite moduli in any case
All residues equal each other; CRT solution is then simply that common residue
questions.explanation: CRT requires pairwise coprime moduli. If not, raise — or extend to handle the generalized non-coprime case explicitly. Silent acceptance of non-coprime moduli is a footgun.

questions.question: A user writes `key = mod_inverse(e, phi)` without checking `gcd(e, phi) == 1`. What's the library's responsibility?
options: Raise an explicit `NoInverseError` from inside mod_inverse — never return garbage silently
Return 0 to signal no inverse exists, letting the caller branch on the result value
Return e itself unchanged so downstream RSA code surfaces the issue eventually
Log a warning but continue computing a meaningless residue; RSA will fail anyway
questions.explanation: Library APIs MUST fail loudly on broken preconditions. Silent 0 / garbage breeds production-RSA disasters (Debian 2008, ROCA 2017). Raise typed exceptions; document them.
